hostPolicyRows.notes: IPv4 loopback is always allowed cleartext.
RFC1918 10.0.0.0/8 is allowed cleartext.
RFC1918 172.16.0.0/12 is allowed cleartext.
RFC1918 192.168.0.0/16 is allowed cleartext. Also the Android LAN-host regression case.
IPv4 link-local 169.254.0.0/16 is allowed cleartext.
IPv6 loopback is always allowed cleartext.
IPv6 unique local address fc00::/7 is allowed cleartext.
IPv6 link-local fe80::/10 is allowed cleartext.
mDNS-style .local names are allowed cleartext.
Single-label DNS names (no dot) are allowed cleartext; they cannot resolve on the public internet.
The literal name 'localhost' is allowed cleartext.
RFC 6598 100.64.0.0/10 is shared address space, not a private LAN (#9474). HTTP is rejected on every native client. IPv6 ULA, including Tailscale fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48, remains allowed.
100.128.0.1 is ordinary public IPv4 outside 100.64.0.0/10 and must not receive cleartext.
Public IPv4 addresses must not receive cleartext traffic.
Public IPv6 literals must not receive cleartext traffic (the bug fixed by #9332).
Multi-label public hostnames must not receive cleartext traffic.

Raw (non-percent-encoded) IPv6 zone IDs are rejected unconditionally, even on an otherwise-private range: the scope is ambiguous outside its originating interface. .NET's Uri.Host silently discards the zone ID; detection instead uses Uri.IdnHost, the one accessor that still carries it.

RFC 6874 percent-encoded IPv6 zone IDs are rejected unconditionally too, matching Swift's blanket guard. Previously allowed by .NET (host reduced to the bare private literal after Uri stripped the zone ID).
A zone ID on an already-public IPv6 literal stays rejected.

IPv4-mapped IPv6 literals (::ffff:a.b.c.d) are rejected outright, even when the mapped address is loopback. Previously allowed by .NET via IPAddress.IsLoopback's IPv4-mapped special case; Swift already rejected every ::ffff:... form.
IPv4-mapped IPv6 literals are rejected outright even when the mapped address is a private range. Already correctly rejected on both platforms; kept as a regression pin.
IPv4-mapped IPv6 literals are rejected outright even when the mapped address is public.
Only http and https schemes are accepted.
Unparsable endpoint text is rejected.
Embedded userinfo is rejected regardless of scheme.
A query string is rejected regardless of scheme (it could leak a credential into logs).
A fragment is rejected regardless of scheme.
The cleartext-only host restriction does not apply to https: any host is allowed once traffic is encrypted.
HTTPS skips the cleartext host gate even on RFC 6598 100.64.0.0/10 (#9474). A later special-case that rejected CGNAT on TLS would fail this row.

Unlike the cleartext-host restriction (which https is exempt from), the zone-ID guard applies regardless of scheme. A zone ID is only meaningful on its originating interface, and allowing it through under https would make the canonical Origin diverge between platforms: .NET's Uri.Host silently drops a zone ID while Swift's URL.host retains it percent-decoded, so the two clients would disagree on the credential-scoping origin for the same endpoint.

originPairs.notes: Implicit and explicit default HTTPS ports must canonicalize identically so credential invalidation on endpoint change is consistent across clients.
Implicit and explicit default HTTP ports must canonicalize identically.
IPv6 hosts must be bracketed in the canonical origin string: an unbracketed 'scheme://host:port' form is ambiguous because the host itself contains colons.
Same IPv6 bracket-canonicalization requirement over https.
